analysis.one_liner: Waives federal wage rules and bike/pedestrian requirements for federally funded highway projects.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote in the House and died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have suspended federal laws and regulations on federally funded highway construction for five years, including the Davis-Bacon rule that requires contractors to pay workers the local prevailing wage. It would also have repealed federal requirements that highway projects accommodate pedestrians and bicyclists, and removed federal funding set-asides for sidewalks and bike facilities. Contractors would have been free to pay lower wages, and states would no longer have been pushed to build walkable, bikeable infrastructure alongside roads.
analysis.who_benefits: Highway construction contractors and road-building companies, who would save money on labor by paying less than the local prevailing wage for five years on federal-aid projects.

how_it_helps.text: Suspends federal requirements, including prevailing-rate-of-pay rules under Davis-Bacon, on federal-aid highway and highway safety construction projects for five years, with exceptions only for laws on highway safety or durability and public or workplace safety [S2][S3].

Repeals the federal prohibition on highway projects that sever or harm routes for nonmotorized traffic unless a reasonable alternative route is provided, and repeals the statutory authorization for spending on pedestrian walkways and bicycle transportation facilities [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federal highway projects, who could be paid less than the local prevailing wage, and pedestrians, cyclists, children, older adults, and people with disabilities, who would lose federal requirements and funding channels for sidewalks and safe walking routes.

drawbacks.text: Waiving prevailing wage rules would cut the pay of construction workers on federal-aid highway projects, directly reducing earnings in a heavily unionized workforce [S2][S3].

Repealing the walkway and bike facility requirements and funding authorization would leave nondrivers — including children, older adults, and people with disabilities — with fewer guaranteed safe routes along federally funded highways [S2][S3].

Supporters would acknowledge the trade-off was deliberate speed and cost over wages and non-driver access: the bill kept an exception for workplace safety and sunset after five years, but the wage and pedestrian provisions were the point of the expedite plan [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — faster, cheaper road construction — would come almost entirely from reducing construction workers' wages and stripping guarantees for people who walk or bike. The savings for contractors and taxpayers were speculative, while the wage cuts and loss of safe routes would be concrete and fell on working people and nondrivers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then its Highways and Transit Subcommittee, and never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Randy Forbes introduced the bill on March 25, 2015 [S1][S5].

It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on March 25, 2015, and to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit the next day, and no further action appears in the record [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Highway construction workers kept prevailing-wage protections, and pedestrian and cyclist funding requirements stayed intact, because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Rep. Randy Forbes
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would waive wage and pedestrian/bicycle requirements on federal highway projects.

against.name: House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure
against.role: Committee of referral; never scheduled action on the bill
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Highways and Transit Subcommittee, where it sat with no markup or vote for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no cosponsors signed on, so the record shows no evidence about how the parties would have lined up [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would exempt federal-aid highway projects from prevailing wage requirements, letting contractors cut labor costs directly out of workers' paychecks for five years [S2][S3].
Repealing the walkway and bike facility authorization and planning requirements would shrink a funding channel these firms build through, alongside the loss of safe routes for the public [S2][S3].
